newsitem.title: GERMANY: Deutsche revamps property business after Schneider.
newsitem.headline: Deutsche revamps property business after Schneider.

text.p: Deutsche Bank AG, Germany's largest bank, said on Wednesday it had reorganised its real estate business to prevent a repeat of the Schneider property debacle of 1994.
The bank announced it had pooled its various commercial real estate activities under a single management in a new division which will comprise a loan volume well in excess of 100 billion marks.

The reorganisation was completed last year and is a reaction to losses resulting from the collapse of the Schneider group with total debts of more than five billion marks in one of Germany's biggest corporate scandals.
Property magnate Juergen Schneider, who is accused of defrauding banks by allegedly obtaining credit on the basis of forged rental contracts, is awaiting trial in a Frankfurt jail.
Deutsche, Schneider's biggest creditor with an exposure of 1.2 billion marks, bore the brunt of public outrage at the apparent ease with which he allegedly duped banks into lending him millions.
Chief executive Hilmar Kopper made matters worse by describing millions of marks in losses to trade creditors as "peanuts" in an off-the-cuff remark.
Four Deutsche executives lost their jobs after an internal investigation into the affair but the bank insisted at the time they had not acted dishonourably.
The new division, Geschaeftsbereich Immobilien (GBI), has uniform standards for processing loan requests as well as joint marketing.

It comprises Deutsche's own commercial property financing business, its giant mortgage subsidiary Frankfurter Hypothekenbank Centralboden (FHC) as well as real estate investment fund companies Deutsche Grundbesitz Investmentgesellschaft (DGI) and Deutsche Immobilien Anlagegesellschaft (DIA).
GBI said it had set up so-called property service centres in eight cities across Germany which offer advice and can decide on the spot whether to extend credit.

Deutsche management board member Michael Endres said the pooling of knowhow on property financing and risk assessement had led to "an optimum linkup which makes it possible to serve the customers far more comprehensively and better."
Deutsche also plans to launch more real estate investment funds this year including a closed, $215 million investment fund for an office building in New York in the next few days, Endres said.
The fund, to be issued by DIA, will pay a return of about seven percent after U.S. taxes.
The new division also includes Deutsche's real estate administration business which covers 385 buildings with 2.6 million square metres of floor space.
